title: OWASP Top 10
subtitle: The ten most critical web application security risks — what they are, how common they are, and how to prevent each one

content.text: OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) is a non-profit foundation that publishes free security resources. Their most famous document is the OWASP Top 10 — a consensus list of the ten most critical security risks for web applications, updated every few years based on data from hundreds of organisations. It's not a law, but it's become the industry benchmark: compliance frameworks, security audits, and job interviews all reference it. Understanding the Top 10 gives you a mental map of the web security landscape.

content.code:
A01 — BROKEN ACCESS CONTROL          (most common, was #5 in 2017)
  Users can act outside their intended permissions
  Example: change ?user_id=123 to ?user_id=456 and see another user's data
  Prevention: deny by default, check permissions server-side, never trust client

A02 — CRYPTOGRAPHIC FAILURES         (was 'Sensitive Data Exposure')
  Weak encryption, plaintext transmission, weak hashing
  Example: storing passwords as MD5 hashes; using HTTP not HTTPS
  Prevention: TLS everywhere, bcrypt for passwords, AES-256 for data at rest

A03 — INJECTION                      (was #1 for many years)
  SQL, NoSQL, OS command, LDAP injection — untrusted data as commands
  Example: ' OR '1'='1 in a login form returning all users
  Prevention: parameterized queries, input validation, escaping

A04 — INSECURE DESIGN
  Missing security controls at design time, not just implementation bugs
  Example: a password-reset flow that asks 'What city were you born in?'
  Prevention: threat modelling, secure design patterns from the start

A05 — SECURITY MISCONFIGURATION      (most common in practice)
  Default passwords, unnecessary features enabled, overly permissive CORS
  Example: debug mode enabled in production, pgAdmin exposed to internet
  Prevention: hardened configs, infrastructure as code, regular audits

A06 — VULNERABLE AND OUTDATED COMPONENTS
  Unpatched libraries, old frameworks, unsupported software
  Example: Equifax breach (Apache Struts), Log4Shell (Log4j)
  Prevention: Dependabot, npm audit, Software Composition Analysis (SCA)

A07 — IDENTIFICATION AND AUTHENTICATION FAILURES
  Weak passwords, broken session management, missing MFA
  Example: session tokens that never expire; no rate limiting on login
  Prevention: strong password policies, MFA, secure session management

A08 — SOFTWARE AND DATA INTEGRITY FAILURES
  Code and data not verified before use; insecure CI/CD pipelines
  Example: auto-updating dependencies without verification (supply chain attack)
  Prevention: code signing, pin dependency versions, review CI/CD permissions

A09 — SECURITY LOGGING AND MONITORING FAILURES
  Not detecting, alerting, or responding to breaches
  Example: an attacker exfiltrates data for 200 days before detection (average)
  Prevention: log security events, alert on anomalies, have an incident plan

A10 — SERVER-SIDE REQUEST FORGERY (SSRF)
  Server fetches a URL provided by the attacker, reaching internal services
  Example: image upload feature fetches http://169.254.169.254/ (AWS metadata)
  Prevention: validate and allowlist URLs, block internal IP ranges

content.text: Risk scoring — how OWASP ranks vulnerabilities

content.code:
Risk = Likelihood × Impact

LIKELIHOOD factors:
  - How easy is it to exploit? (SQL injection in a text box = easy)
  - How common is it? (Broken access control = extremely common)
  - How detectable is the attack? (SQL errors visible = easy to detect)

IMPACT factors:
  - What data can be accessed? (all user records = high)
  - What actions can be taken? (admin access = critical)
  - Business impact (GDPR fine, reputation damage, legal liability)

CRITICAL:  Broken access control to admin panel (high likelihood, high impact)
HIGH:      SQL injection in a search box (medium likelihood, high impact)
MEDIUM:    Missing CSRF token on a low-value form
LOW:       Missing security header with no immediate exploit

content.text: A06 (Vulnerable Components) is the easiest win. Run npm audit in your project right now. If you have high or critical vulnerabilities, run npm audit fix. Enable Dependabot on GitHub (it's free) and it will open PRs when your dependencies have security patches. This one automation addresses A06 entirely and takes 5 minutes to set up. Most teams skip it and get breached by vulnerabilities that had patches available for months.

questions.question: A developer builds an admin dashboard and checks permissions with: 'if (user.isAdmin) { showAdminPanel() }' — but only in the frontend JavaScript. The API endpoints still return data for any authenticated user. Which OWASP category is this?
options: A03 — Injection, because data is not being sanitised
A01 — Broken Access Control, because authorisation is enforced only on the client, not the server
A05 — Security Misconfiguration, because admin features should be disabled
questions.explanation: This is A01 — Broken Access Control. Checking permissions only in the frontend JavaScript is worthless: an attacker opens the browser DevTools, calls the API directly (or modifies the JavaScript), and bypasses the check entirely. Access control must ALWAYS be enforced on the server. The API endpoint must verify the requesting user has admin privileges before returning data, regardless of what the client claims. 'Never trust the client' is the golden rule of web security.

faq.q: Does passing OWASP Top 10 mean my app is secure?
faq.a: No — it means you've addressed the most common vulnerabilities, which puts you ahead of most apps. The Top 10 is a minimum bar, not a complete security standard. It doesn't cover business logic flaws (which are app-specific), cryptographic implementation details, physical security, or many advanced attack techniques. After the Top 10, consider SOC 2, ISO 27001, or a penetration test for a more thorough assessment.

examples: PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry standard — required if you process card payments) explicitly references OWASP Top 10. If you want to process payments without a third-party processor, your app must pass a PCI security assessment that checks for OWASP vulnerabilities

GitHub's Security Advisory Database tracks CVEs in open-source packages. In 2023, over 2,000 npm packages were found to have critical vulnerabilities. The vast majority were A06 (Vulnerable Components) — fixed by updating the package, never fixed because no one checked
